meta.source: Curated questions; answer coordinates from the English Wikipedia article for each site.

questions.q: Alexander Fleming noticed mould killing bacteria in a Petri dish — the discovery of penicillin. Where was his laboratory?
questions.why: Fleming worked in a small laboratory at St Mary’s Hospital Medical School in Paddington. The room is preserved today as the Alexander Fleming Laboratory Museum.

questions.q: Francis Crick and James Watson built their model of the DNA double helix at which university laboratory?
questions.why: Watson and Crick worked at the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge, drawing on X-ray data from Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins at King’s College London. The model was published in Nature in April 1953.

questions.q: Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays while experimenting with cathode-ray tubes. In which university city was his laboratory?
questions.why: Röntgen made the discovery in November 1895 at the University of Würzburg’s physics institute, and won the first Nobel Prize in Physics for it in 1901.

questions.q: Marie and Pierre Curie discovered polonium and radium working in a converted shed at which school?
questions.a: ESPCI (School of Industrial Physics and Chemistry)
questions.why: The Curies worked in a draughty shed at the École municipale de physique et de chimie industrielles (today ESPCI Paris), where they announced polonium and then radium in 1898.

questions.q: Galileo first saw four moons orbiting Jupiter through his telescope while he was a professor in which city?
questions.why: Galileo taught at the University of Padua from 1592 to 1610, and observed the Galilean moons there in January 1610 before publishing them in Sidereus Nuncius.

questions.q: Edward Jenner performed the first smallpox vaccination, using cowpox, on eight-year-old James Phipps. In which village did he practise?
questions.why: Jenner was a country doctor in Berkeley, Gloucestershire. His home there, The Chantry, is now Dr Jenner’s House museum.

questions.q: Frederick Banting and Charles Best first isolated insulin, transforming the treatment of diabetes. At which university?
questions.why: Banting and Best did the work in J.J.R. Macleod’s laboratory at the University of Toronto in 1921; Banting and Macleod shared the 1923 Nobel Prize.

questions.q: Christiaan Barnard led the team that carried out the world’s first human-to-human heart transplant. In which city?
questions.why: The operation on Louis Washkansky took place at Groote Schuur Hospital in Cape Town on 3 December 1967.

questions.q: Louise Brown, the world’s first baby conceived by IVF, was born at which hospital?
questions.why: Louise Brown was born at Oldham General Hospital (now the Royal Oldham Hospital) on 25 July 1978, after pioneering work by Robert Edwards and Patrick Steptoe.

questions.q: Dolly the sheep, the first mammal cloned from an adult cell, was created at which research institute?
questions.why: Dolly was born on 5 July 1996 at the Roslin Institute, just south of Edinburgh. She is now on display at the National Museum of Scotland.

questions.q: Ernest Rutherford announced the discovery of the atomic nucleus after the gold-foil experiment. At which university did he do it?
questions.why: Rutherford interpreted Geiger and Marsden’s gold-foil results at the Victoria University of Manchester, publishing the nuclear model of the atom in 1911.

questions.q: Gregor Mendel worked out the laws of inheritance by breeding pea plants in the garden of his monastery. Where?
questions.why: Mendel’s experiments (1856–1863) took place at the Augustinian St Thomas’s Abbey in Brno, then in the Austrian Empire; he presented the results in 1865.

questions.q: Edwin Hubble’s observations showing the universe is expanding were made with the 100-inch Hooker telescope at which observatory?
questions.why: The Hooker telescope on Mount Wilson, above Pasadena, was the world’s largest from 1917 to 1949. Hubble published his velocity–distance relation in 1929.

questions.q: William Herschel discovered the planet Uranus with a homemade telescope in the garden of his house. In which city?
questions.why: Herschel spotted Uranus from 19 New King Street, Bath, on 13 March 1781 — the first planet discovered with a telescope. The house is now the Herschel Museum of Astronomy.

questions.q: The 1884 International Meridian Conference chose the line through which observatory as the world’s prime meridian, 0° longitude?
questions.why: Delegates from 25 nations meeting in Washington, D.C., chose the meridian through the Airy transit circle at the Royal Observatory, Greenwich.

questions.q: Tycho Brahe built Uraniborg, the most precise naked-eye observatory of its age, on an island in the strait between Denmark and Sweden. Which island?
questions.why: King Frederick II granted Tycho the island of Hven (Ven) in 1576. His measurements there underpinned Kepler’s laws of planetary motion.

questions.q: The astronomer-sultan Ulugh Beg built a vast observatory in the 1420s whose star catalogue was the best for two centuries. In which city?
questions.why: Ulugh Beg’s observatory on a hill outside Samarkand housed an enormous meridian arc; its remains were rediscovered in 1908.

questions.q: Felix Hoffmann synthesised a stable form of acetylsalicylic acid — aspirin — at the Bayer company’s laboratories. In which city were they?
questions.why: Bayer’s laboratories were then in Elberfeld, today part of Wuppertal. Aspirin was registered as a trademark in 1899.

questions.q: The last naturally occurring case of smallpox in the world was recorded in a hospital cook named Ali Maow Maalin. In which town?
questions.why: Ali Maow Maalin fell ill in Merca, Somalia, in October 1977. The WHO declared smallpox eradicated in 1980.

questions.q: Johannes Gutenberg developed printing with movable metal type and printed his famous Bible in his home city. Which city?
questions.why: Gutenberg developed his press in Strasbourg and Mainz, and printed the Gutenberg Bible in Mainz around 1455. The Gutenberg Museum is there today.

questions.q: “Mr. Watson — come here — I want to see you.” Alexander Graham Bell made the first successful telephone call to his assistant in which city?
questions.why: Bell made the call on 10 March 1876 from his workshop at 5 Exeter Place, Boston, three days after his telephone patent was granted.

questions.q: Thomas Edison’s team demonstrated a long-lasting carbon-filament light bulb at his “invention factory”. Where was it?
questions.why: Edison’s Menlo Park laboratory in Raritan Township (today Edison, New Jersey) gave him the nickname “the Wizard of Menlo Park”; the lamp was shown publicly on New Year’s Eve 1879.

questions.q: John Bardeen, Walter Brattain and William Shockley built the first working transistor at which research laboratory?
questions.why: The point-contact transistor was demonstrated at Bell Telephone Laboratories in Murray Hill, New Jersey, in December 1947; the trio shared the 1956 Nobel Prize.

questions.q: Tim Berners-Lee proposed — and then built — the World Wide Web while working at which research centre?
questions.why: Berners-Lee wrote his proposal at CERN in March 1989 and had the first web server running there by the end of 1990.

questions.q: The first message ever sent over ARPANET, the forerunner of the internet, left a computer on which university campus?
questions.why: On 29 October 1969, Charley Kline at UCLA tried to type “LOGIN” to the Stanford Research Institute; the system crashed after “LO”.

questions.q: Colossus, the world’s first programmable electronic digital computer, was put to work breaking German codes at which wartime site?
questions.why: Colossus, designed by Tommy Flowers, began work at Bletchley Park in early 1944 against the Lorenz cipher.

questions.q: The oldest surviving camera photograph, “View from the Window at Le Gras”, was taken by Nicéphore Niépce at his country estate. Near which village?
questions.why: Niépce made the image from an upstairs window of his estate, Le Gras, at Saint-Loup-de-Varennes near Chalon-sur-Saône, around 1826–27.

questions.q: Carl Benz built the Patent-Motorwagen, generally regarded as the first practical petrol-powered car, in his workshop in which city?
questions.why: Benz built the car in Mannheim in 1885 and patented it in January 1886. In 1888 Bertha Benz drove it from Mannheim to Pforzheim — the first long-distance car journey.

questions.q: The earliest known patent application for a telescope was filed in 1608 by spectacle-maker Hans Lipperhey. In which city did he work?
questions.why: Lipperhey, a lens-maker in Middelburg, applied to the States General for a patent in October 1608. It was refused — others claimed the idea too.

questions.q: “What hath God wrought” — Samuel Morse sent the first long-distance telegraph message on the Washington–Baltimore line. From which building?
questions.why: Morse sent the message on 24 May 1844 from the Supreme Court chamber in the Capitol to Alfred Vail in Baltimore.

questions.q: Guglielmo Marconi received the first transatlantic radio signal — the letter “S” in Morse — on a hill above which harbour city?
questions.why: On 12 December 1901 Marconi heard the signal from Poldhu, Cornwall, using a kite-borne aerial at Signal Hill, St. John’s.

questions.q: Richard Arkwright built the world’s first water-powered cotton-spinning mill, a blueprint for the factory system. In which Derbyshire village?
questions.why: Arkwright’s Cromford Mill opened in 1771 on the River Derwent and is part of the Derwent Valley Mills World Heritage Site.

questions.q: Henry Ford introduced the first moving assembly line for whole cars, building the Model T, at which plant?
questions.why: The moving line began at Highland Park, just north of Detroit, in 1913, cutting Model T assembly from about 12 hours to about 90 minutes.

questions.q: The Montgolfier brothers gave the first public demonstration of a hot-air balloon in the square of their home town. Which town?
questions.why: On 4 June 1783 an unmanned Montgolfier balloon rose from Annonay’s market square; crewed flights followed in Paris later that year.

questions.q: Momofuku Ando invented instant ramen — Chikin Ramen — in a shed behind his house. In which city?
questions.why: Ando perfected flash-fried noodles in Ikeda, Osaka, in 1958. The Cupnoodles Museum Osaka Ikeda stands there today.

questions.q: Motorola’s Martin Cooper made the first public call from a handheld mobile phone while walking down a street in which city?
questions.why: Cooper called a rival at Bell Labs from Sixth Avenue in Manhattan on 3 April 1973, using a prototype DynaTAC.

questions.q: Orville and Wilbur Wright made the first powered, controlled aeroplane flights on 17 December 1903. Where?
questions.a: Kill Devil Hills, near Kitty Hawk
questions.why: The Wrights chose the windy dunes of Kill Devil Hills on the Outer Banks, near the village of Kitty Hawk. The first flight lasted 12 seconds.

questions.q: Apollo 11, the mission that put the first people on the Moon, lifted off from Launch Complex 39A. Where is it?
questions.why: Apollo 11 launched from Pad 39A at Kennedy Space Center on Merritt Island, Florida, on 16 July 1969.

questions.q: Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite, was launched from which cosmodrome?
questions.why: Sputnik 1 launched on 4 October 1957 from the Soviet test range at Tyuratam — now Baikonur, leased by Russia from Kazakhstan. Gagarin flew from the same pad in 1961.

questions.q: Alcock and Brown completed the first non-stop transatlantic flight in 1919, crash-landing nose-first in a bog. Near which town?
questions.why: After 16 hours from St John’s, Newfoundland, their Vickers Vimy landed in Derrygimlagh bog near Clifden, mistaking it for a field.

questions.q: Yang Liwei became China’s first astronaut when Shenzhou 5 launched from which launch centre?
questions.why: Shenzhou 5 launched on 15 October 2003 from Jiuquan, in the Gobi Desert, making China the third country to fly a person into space on its own rocket.

questions.q: Chandrayaan-3, the first mission to land near the Moon’s south pole, launched from which space centre?
questions.why: ISRO launched Chandrayaan-3 from Sriharikota island on 14 July 2023; its Vikram lander touched down on 23 August.

questions.q: Concorde, the supersonic airliner, made its very first flight on 2 March 1969 from which city’s airport?
questions.why: Prototype 001 took off from Toulouse–Blagnac with André Turcat at the controls; the British prototype first flew from Filton a month later.

questions.q: The first nuclear weapon test, codenamed Trinity, took place on 16 July 1945. In which US state?
questions.a: Trinity site, Jornada del Muerto desert
questions.why: The test was carried out in the Jornada del Muerto desert on what is now the White Sands Missile Range, south of the Manhattan Project’s Los Alamos laboratory.

questions.q: Enrico Fermi’s team achieved the first man-made self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction in a squash court beneath a stadium. Where?
questions.why: Chicago Pile-1 went critical on 2 December 1942 under the stands of Stagg Field at the University of Chicago.

questions.q: The world’s first nuclear power station to supply electricity to a public grid opened in 1954. In which Soviet science town?
questions.why: The 5 MW Obninsk plant, south-west of Moscow, was connected to the grid on 26 June 1954.

questions.q: The Home Insurance Building, often called the first skyscraper for its load-bearing steel frame, was completed in 1885 in which city?
questions.why: William Le Baron Jenney’s ten-storey building stood at LaSalle and Adams streets in Chicago until 1931.

questions.q: The world’s first major bridge made of cast iron was erected in 1779 across the River Severn. In which county?
questions.why: Abraham Darby III built the Iron Bridge near Coalbrookdale, where his grandfather had pioneered smelting iron with coke.

questions.q: Stephenson’s Rocket won the trials held to choose locomotives for the Liverpool and Manchester Railway. Where were they held?
questions.why: The Rainhill Trials ran in October 1829 on a level stretch of the new line at Rainhill, east of Liverpool.

questions.q: The Althing, often called the world’s oldest surviving parliament, first met in the open air in 930 CE. Where?
questions.why: Iceland’s chieftains met at Þingvellir, in a rift valley where the North American and Eurasian plates pull apart, until 1798.

questions.q: Founded by Fatima al-Fihri in 859, it is recognised by UNESCO and Guinness as the oldest continually operating university. In which city?
questions.why: Al-Qarawiyyin began as a mosque in the medina of Fez and grew into a centre of learning; it became part of Morocco’s state university system in 1963.

questions.q: The Diamond Sutra, the world’s oldest dated printed book (868 CE), was found sealed in a “library cave” in 1900. Near which oasis town?
questions.why: The Taoist monk Wang Yuanlu found the sealed Library Cave at the Mogao Caves outside Dunhuang, on the Silk Road.

questions.q: King John agreed to Magna Carta in June 1215 at a water-meadow beside the Thames. Where?
questions.why: The charter was agreed at Runnymede, between Windsor and Staines, on 15 June 1215.

questions.q: The US Declaration of Independence was adopted and signed in the Pennsylvania State House. In which city?
questions.why: The Second Continental Congress adopted the Declaration in the State House, now Independence Hall, on 4 July 1776.

questions.q: Napoleon’s final defeat came at the Battle of Waterloo in June 1815. In which present-day country was it fought?
questions.why: The battle was fought south of the town of Waterloo, then in the United Kingdom of the Netherlands and now in Belgium.

questions.q: Archduke Franz Ferdinand was assassinated beside the Latin Bridge, the spark for the First World War. In which city?
questions.why: Gavrilo Princip shot the Archduke and his wife Sophie on 28 June 1914 at the corner beside Sarajevo’s Latin Bridge.

questions.q: The armistice ending the fighting of the First World War was signed in a railway carriage in a forest. Near which French town?
questions.why: The armistice was signed in Marshal Foch’s carriage in the Forest of Compiègne at 5 a.m. on 11 November 1918.

questions.q: The treaty formally ending the First World War with Germany was signed in the Hall of Mirrors. In which palace?
questions.why: The Treaty of Versailles was signed on 28 June 1919, five years to the day after the Sarajevo assassination.

questions.q: The United Nations Charter was signed by 50 nations on 26 June 1945. In which city?
questions.why: The charter was drawn up at the San Francisco Conference and signed at the Veterans War Memorial Building next to the Opera House.

questions.q: Truman, Stalin and Churchill (then Attlee) decided the shape of post-war Europe in the summer of 1945 at a palace in which city?
questions.why: The Potsdam Conference met at Cecilienhof Palace from 17 July to 2 August 1945.

questions.q: Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin met at a former tsar’s summer palace in February 1945 to plan the end of the Second World War. Where?
questions.why: The Yalta Conference took place at Livadia Palace on the Black Sea coast of Crimea, 4–11 February 1945.

questions.q: In October 1917 the Bolsheviks stormed the Winter Palace, seat of Russia’s Provisional Government. In which city?
questions.why: The palace, now part of the Hermitage Museum, was taken on the night of 25–26 October 1917 (Old Style).

questions.q: The world’s worst nuclear power accident happened at Reactor No. 4 on 26 April 1986. Where?
questions.why: The plant lies beside the abandoned city of Pripyat in northern Ukraine, close to the border with Belarus.

questions.q: Gandhi’s Salt March ended when he picked up a lump of natural salt on the shore, defying British law. At which coastal village?
questions.why: Gandhi walked about 385 km from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi on the Arabian Sea, arriving on 6 April 1930.

questions.q: Nelson Mandela spent 18 of his 27 years in prison on an island off which city?
questions.place: Table Bay, Cape Town, South Africa
questions.why: Mandela was held on Robben Island from 1964 to 1982. The island is now a museum and World Heritage Site.

questions.q: On 16 June 1976 students protesting against compulsory Afrikaans lessons were shot by police, starting an uprising. In which township?
questions.why: The Soweto uprising is commemorated each year on 16 June as Youth Day in South Africa.

questions.q: Leaders of 29 newly independent Asian and African nations met in 1955 in a conference that founded the Non-Aligned Movement. In which city?
questions.why: The Asian–African Conference met at the Gedung Merdeka in Bandung in April 1955.

questions.q: The Organisation of African Unity, forerunner of the African Union, was founded in 1963 in which capital?
questions.why: Thirty-two states signed the OAU Charter in Addis Ababa on 25 May 1963, now celebrated as Africa Day. The African Union is still headquartered there.

questions.q: Kwame Nkrumah declared the first independence of a sub-Saharan African colony from European rule at midnight on 6 March 1957. In which city?
questions.why: Nkrumah announced Ghana’s independence at the Old Polo Grounds in Accra: “Ghana, your beloved country, is free for ever.”

questions.q: Emperor Menelik II’s army defeated an Italian invasion force in 1896, securing Ethiopia’s independence. Near which town?
questions.why: The Battle of Adwa (1 March 1896) made Ethiopia one of only two African countries never colonised.

questions.q: At the opening battle of the Anglo-Zulu War, a Zulu army inflicted a crushing defeat on British forces beneath a distinctive rocky hill. Which?
questions.why: On 22 January 1879 about 20,000 Zulu warriors overran the British camp at Isandlwana.

questions.q: Jean-Jacques Dessalines proclaimed Haiti’s independence — the only nation born of a successful slave revolt — on 1 January 1804. In which town?
questions.why: The Act of Independence was read in Gonaïves, known as the “City of Independence”.

questions.q: Father Miguel Hidalgo rang his church bell and issued the “Grito”, the cry that began Mexico’s War of Independence. In which town?
questions.why: Hidalgo’s Grito de Dolores on 16 September 1810 is re-enacted every year on the eve of Mexico’s Independence Day.

questions.q: Simón Bolívar’s victory at a bridge in the Andes in August 1819 secured the independence of New Granada (today Colombia). Where?
questions.why: The Battle of Boyacá was fought on 7 August 1819 at a bridge over the Teatinos River south of Tunja.

questions.q: Egypt’s Anwar Sadat and Israel’s Menachem Begin agreed a framework for peace in 1978 at the US president’s country retreat. Where is it?
questions.why: Jimmy Carter hosted 13 days of talks at Camp David in the Catoctin Mountains in September 1978.

questions.q: The armistice that halted the Korean War was signed in 1953 in a village on the line between the two armies. Which?
questions.why: The armistice was signed at Panmunjom on 27 July 1953; the Joint Security Area there is still where the two Koreas meet.

questions.q: Japan formally surrendered, ending the Second World War, aboard the battleship USS Missouri on 2 September 1945. Where was the ship anchored?
questions.why: The ceremony took place on the Missouri’s deck in Tokyo Bay, with General MacArthur accepting the surrender for the Allies.

questions.q: The siege that ended French colonial rule in Indochina in 1954 took place in a remote valley. Where?
questions.why: General Võ Nguyên Giáp’s Viet Minh forces captured the French garrison at Điện Biên Phủ on 7 May 1954, leading to the Geneva Accords.

questions.q: Robert Clive’s victory over the Nawab of Bengal in 1757 began British rule in India. Near which village was the battle fought?
questions.why: The Battle of Plassey on 23 June 1757 was fought beside the Bhagirathi River, north of Calcutta.

questions.q: The treaty ending the First Opium War, which ceded Hong Kong Island to Britain, was signed aboard HMS Cornwallis off which city?
questions.why: The Treaty of Nanking was signed on 29 August 1842 on the Yangtze at Nanjing.

questions.q: Spain and Portugal divided the newly explored lands outside Europe between them with a treaty signed in 1494. In which Spanish town?
questions.why: The Treaty of Tordesillas drew a line 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands; it was signed on 7 June 1494.

questions.q: The Treaty of Waitangi, New Zealand’s founding document, was first signed by British officials and Māori chiefs in February 1840. Where?
questions.why: The first signatures were made on 6 February 1840 at Waitangi in the Bay of Islands; the day is now New Zealand’s national holiday.

questions.q: The First Fleet established Britain’s first colony in Australia on 26 January 1788. At which cove?
questions.why: Arthur Phillip moved the fleet from Botany Bay to Sydney Cove in Port Jackson, which offered fresh water and deep anchorage.

questions.q: Gold miners built a stockade and rebelled against colonial authorities in 1854 — the Eureka Rebellion. In which goldfields town?
questions.why: Troops overran the Eureka Stockade at Ballarat on 3 December 1854; the miners’ demands later helped bring democratic reform to Victoria.

questions.q: William of Normandy defeated King Harold II in 1066 near a town now named after the battle. Where?
questions.why: The Battle of Hastings was fought about 10 km north-west of Hastings; William built Battle Abbey on the site.

questions.q: Columbus set sail on his first voyage across the Atlantic on 3 August 1492 from which Andalusian port?
questions.why: The Niña, Pinta and Santa María left Palos on the Río Tinto, near the monastery of La Rábida where Columbus had won support.

questions.q: Charles Darwin’s observations of finches, tortoises and mockingbirds on HMS Beagle’s voyage were made on which islands?
questions.why: The Beagle spent five weeks in the Galápagos in 1835; the islands’ variation between species helped shape Darwin’s theory of evolution.

questions.q: Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary stood on top of the world on 29 May 1953. Drop your pin on the summit.
questions.why: The pair climbed via the South Col route from Nepal. Everest’s summit, 8,849 m, lies on the border between Nepal and Tibet.

questions.q: Ferdinand Magellan was killed in battle against the warriors of Lapulapu during the first circumnavigation. On which island?
questions.why: Magellan died at Mactan on 27 April 1521. Juan Sebastián Elcano completed the voyage back to Spain in 1522.

questions.q: Vasco da Gama completed the first sea voyage from Europe to India in May 1498, landing near which city?
questions.why: Da Gama’s ships anchored off Kappad, near Calicut on the Malabar Coast, on 20 May 1498.

questions.q: Captain James Cook was killed in a confrontation on the shore of a bay during his third Pacific voyage. Where?
questions.why: Cook died at Kealakekua Bay on 14 February 1779; a white obelisk marks the spot.

questions.q: “Dr. Livingstone, I presume?” Henry Morton Stanley found the missing explorer in 1871 in a town on Lake Tanganyika. Which?
questions.why: Stanley reached Ujiji, on the eastern shore of Lake Tanganyika, on 10 November 1871.

questions.q: Robert Ballard’s expedition found the wreck of the Titanic in 1985, 73 years after she sank. Drop your pin on the wreck.
questions.why: The wreck lies about 3,800 m down, roughly 600 km south-east of Newfoundland.

questions.q: The Mayflower’s Pilgrims founded their colony in December 1620 at a harbour they named after their English port of departure. Where?
questions.why: After first anchoring off Cape Cod, the Pilgrims settled at Plymouth, named after Plymouth in Devon.

questions.q: The first permanent English settlement in the Americas was founded in May 1607 on a river island in which future state?
questions.why: The Virginia Company’s colonists built James Fort on Jamestown Island on the James River.

questions.q: The only confirmed Norse settlement in North America, from around 1000 CE, was found in 1960. Where?
questions.why: Helge and Anne Stine Ingstad identified the site at the northern tip of Newfoundland; tree rings date Norse wood-cutting there to 1021 CE.

questions.q: Thor Heyerdahl’s balsa raft Kon-Tiki ended its 101-day drift from Peru by crashing onto a reef. Which atoll?
questions.why: The raft wrecked on the reef of Raroia on 7 August 1947, after about 6,900 km at sea.

questions.q: Amelia Earhart and Fred Noonan were last seen alive taking off on 2 July 1937 from which airfield?
questions.why: They left Lae for Howland Island, 4,100 km away, and disappeared over the central Pacific.

questions.q: Hiram Bingham brought this 15th-century Inca citadel to international attention in 1911 — though local farmers already knew it well. Where is it?
questions.why: Machu Picchu sits on a ridge above the Urubamba valley; local guide Melchor Arteaga led Bingham there.

questions.q: The last spike of the Canadian Pacific Railway, linking Canada coast to coast, was driven in 1885 in which mountain province?
questions.why: Donald Smith drove the last spike at Craigellachie in Eagle Pass on 7 November 1885.

questions.q: French soldiers found the Rosetta Stone — the key to deciphering hieroglyphs — in 1799. Near which town in the Nile Delta?
questions.why: The stone was found while rebuilding Fort Julien near Rashid (Rosetta). Champollion announced his decipherment in 1822.

questions.q: Howard Carter found the almost intact tomb of Tutankhamun in November 1922. Where?
questions.why: Tomb KV62 lies in the Valley of the Kings on the west bank of the Nile, opposite Luxor.

questions.q: Farmers digging a well in 1974 found the first figures of the Terracotta Army. Near which city?
questions.why: The army guards the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor of China, at Lintong, about 35 km east of Xi’an.

questions.q: A Bedouin shepherd found the first Dead Sea Scrolls in a cave in 1947. Where?
questions.place: West Bank, near the Dead Sea
questions.why: Over the following decade fragments of about 900 manuscripts were found in eleven caves around Khirbet Qumran.

questions.q: Donald Johanson and Tom Gray found “Lucy”, a 3.2-million-year-old Australopithecus skeleton, in 1974. In which country?
questions.why: Lucy was found at Hadar in the Awash valley of Ethiopia’s Afar Triangle; she is kept at the National Museum in Addis Ababa.

questions.q: Mary and Louis Leakey’s finds of early human fossils and stone tools made which gorge famous as a “cradle of humankind”?
questions.why: Olduvai Gorge, in the Great Rift Valley, has yielded fossils and tools spanning about two million years.

questions.q: A Roman town buried by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 CE has been excavated since 1748. Where?
questions.why: Pompeii lies about 10 km south-east of Vesuvius, near Naples; ash preserved the town in remarkable detail.

questions.q: Four teenagers following their dog discovered caves full of 17,000-year-old paintings of horses and bulls in 1940. Where?
questions.why: The cave near Montignac was closed to the public in 1963 to protect the paintings; replicas are shown nearby.

questions.q: Eight-year-old María Sanz de Sautuola looked up and saw painted bison on a cave ceiling in 1879 — the first prehistoric cave art to be recognised. Where?
questions.why: Altamira, near Santillana del Mar, was at first dismissed as a forgery; it was accepted only in 1902.

questions.q: Hikers found Ötzi, a 5,300-year-old natural mummy, melting out of a glacier in 1991. In which mountain range?
questions.why: Ötzi was found at 3,210 m on the Similaun, just on the Italian side of the border; he is displayed in Bolzano.

questions.q: An Anglo-Saxon ship burial packed with treasure, including a famous helmet, was excavated in 1939. Where?
questions.why: Basil Brown excavated the burial for landowner Edith Pretty; it is thought to be the grave of King Rædwald of East Anglia.

questions.q: Excavations from 1995 revealed carved stone pillars about 11,000 years old — the world’s oldest known megaliths. Where?
questions.why: Klaus Schmidt led excavations at Göbekli Tepe in south-eastern Turkey; it predates Stonehenge by about 6,000 years.

questions.q: Leonard Woolley excavated the Royal Cemetery with its golden treasures and the Standard of Ur. In which modern country?
questions.why: Ur was a great Sumerian city near the old course of the Euphrates in southern Iraq; Woolley dug there from 1922 to 1934.

questions.q: The stele carrying the Code of Hammurabi, one of the oldest written law codes, was found in 1901 far from Babylon. At which ancient city?
questions.why: An Elamite king had carried the stele off to Susa as plunder in the 12th century BCE; Jacques de Morgan’s team found it there. It is now in the Louvre.

questions.q: Some of the earliest known writing — proto-cuneiform tablets from around 3300 BCE — comes from the Mesopotamian city of Uruk. Where was it?
questions.why: Uruk, in southern Iraq, was perhaps the largest city in the world around 3000 BCE, and the home of the legendary king Gilgamesh.

questions.q: One of the largest cities of the Indus Valley Civilisation, with a famous Great Bath, was excavated from the 1920s. Where?
questions.why: Mohenjo-daro, beside the Indus in Sindh, was built around 2500 BCE and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

questions.q: Sponge divers recovered a corroded lump of bronze gears from a Roman-era shipwreck in 1901 — an ancient Greek astronomical calculator. Off which island?
questions.why: The wreck lies off Antikythera, between Kythera and Crete. The mechanism, about 2,100 years old, is in the National Archaeological Museum in Athens.

questions.q: Builders digging foundations in 1938 uncovered superb naturalistic brass heads made by the Yoruba centuries earlier. In which city?
questions.why: The Ife heads, from the 12th–15th centuries, were found in Ile-Ife, the sacred city of Yoruba tradition.

questions.q: The 42,000-year-old remains of “Mungo Man”, among the oldest human remains in Australia, were found in 1974 beside a dry lake. In which state?
questions.why: Jim Bowler found the remains at Lake Mungo in the Willandra Lakes region; they were returned to Country in 2017.

questions.q: Distinctive stone spear points found among mammoth bones gave their name to the Clovis culture of the first Americans. In which US state?
questions.why: The type site at Blackwater Draw, near Clovis and Portales, was excavated from the 1930s.

questions.q: Two pits full of giant bronze masks from a lost Bronze Age culture were discovered in 1986. In which Chinese province?
questions.why: Sanxingdui, near Guanghan, belonged to the ancient kingdom of Shu; its bronzes look like nothing else from early China.

questions.q: A small temple carved into a fortress hill holds one of the earliest dated inscriptions using a round symbol for zero (876 CE). In which city?
questions.why: The Chaturbhuj Temple at Gwalior Fort records a garden 270 hastas long and a gift of 50 garlands, both written with a zero.

questions.q: The greatest library of the ancient world was founded under the Ptolemies around 285 BCE. In which city?
questions.why: The Library of Alexandria stood in the royal quarter of the city founded by Alexander the Great on the Mediterranean coast.

questions.q: Which city in the Andes was the capital of the Inca Empire?
questions.why: Cusco was the Inca capital until the Spanish conquest; Inca stonework still forms the base of many colonial buildings.

questions.q: The Aztec capital Tenochtitlan was built on an island in Lake Texcoco. Which modern city stands on its ruins?
questions.why: The ruins of the Templo Mayor, the Aztecs’ great temple, were uncovered beside Mexico City’s Zócalo from 1978.

questions.q: A “rich mountain” of silver found in 1545 made one of the largest cities in the world in the 1600s. Where?
questions.why: Silver from Cerro Rico in Potosí funded the Spanish Empire for two centuries, at a terrible cost to the forced labourers who mined it.

questions.q: Completed in 1936, this dam on the Colorado River created Lake Mead. Where is it?
questions.why: Hoover Dam stands in Black Canyon on the Nevada–Arizona border, about 50 km south-east of Las Vegas.

questions.q: The world’s largest power station by installed capacity is a dam across the Yangtze. Where is it?
questions.why: The dam at Sandouping, near Yichang, was structurally complete in 2006 and fully operational in 2012.

questions.q: For decades the world’s most productive hydroelectric plant, this dam on the Paraná was built jointly by two countries. Where?
questions.why: Itaipu began generating in 1984 on the Paraná River, a few kilometres north of the Iguazu–Paraná confluence.

questions.q: A high dam completed in 1970 tamed the Nile’s annual floods and created Lake Nasser. Where is it?
questions.why: The dam just south of Aswan created Lake Nasser; the Abu Simbel temples were moved to escape its waters.

questions.q: Completed in 1959, this dam on the Zambezi created what is still the world’s largest artificial reservoir by volume. Where?
questions.why: Kariba Dam spans the Kariba Gorge on the Zambezi, forming Lake Kariba.

questions.q: The world’s tallest building, 828 m high, opened in 2010. Where is it?
questions.why: Burj Khalifa stands in Downtown Dubai and has held the title of world’s tallest building since its completion.

questions.q: Twin 88-storey towers that were the world’s tallest buildings from 1998 to 2004 stand in which city?
questions.why: Designed by César Pelli, the towers are joined by a skybridge on the 41st and 42nd floors.

questions.q: Designed from scratch by Lúcio Costa and Oscar Niemeyer, this city became a national capital in 1960. Where?
questions.why: Brasília replaced Rio de Janeiro as Brazil’s capital to draw development into the interior; its plan resembles an aeroplane.

questions.q: A purpose-built capital designed by Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin was founded in 1913. Where?
questions.why: Canberra was chosen as a compromise between rivals Sydney and Melbourne; Parliament moved there in 1927.

questions.q: The tallest structure in the world from 1889 to 1930 was built as the entrance arch to a World’s Fair. Where?
questions.why: Gustave Eiffel’s company built the tower on the Champ de Mars for the 1889 Exposition Universelle.

questions.q: Michelangelo painted the ceiling of which chapel between 1508 and 1512?
questions.why: The Sistine Chapel is in the Apostolic Palace in Vatican City; papal conclaves still meet beneath Michelangelo’s ceiling.

questions.q: A volcanic eruption in August 1883 was heard nearly 5,000 km away and its tsunamis killed more than 36,000 people. Where was the volcano?
questions.why: Krakatoa lies in the Sunda Strait between Java and Sumatra. Anak Krakatau, “child of Krakatoa”, rose from the caldera in 1927.

questions.q: The largest volcanic eruption in recorded history, in 1815, caused the “Year Without a Summer” in 1816. Which volcano?
questions.why: Tambora, on Sumbawa island, threw so much ash and sulphur into the stratosphere that harvests failed across the Northern Hemisphere.

questions.q: On All Saints’ Day 1755 an earthquake, tsunami and fires destroyed much of a European capital. Which?
questions.why: The Great Lisbon Earthquake of 1 November 1755 killed tens of thousands and shook Enlightenment thinkers, including Voltaire.

questions.q: The most powerful earthquake ever recorded — magnitude 9.5 — struck on 22 May 1960 near which city?
questions.why: The Great Chilean Earthquake was centred near Valdivia; its tsunami reached Hawaii and Japan.

questions.q: Known as the “wickedest city on Earth”, this pirate haven largely slid into the sea in an earthquake in 1692. Where?
questions.why: Port Royal sat at the tip of the Palisadoes spit; about two-thirds of the town sank on 7 June 1692.

questions.q: In 1908 an exploding space rock flattened about 80 million trees across 2,000 km² of forest. In which region?
questions.why: The air burst over the Podkamennaya Tunguska River on 30 June 1908 is the largest impact event in recorded history.

questions.q: The buried impact crater linked to the extinction of the dinosaurs 66 million years ago was confirmed in 1991. Where is its centre?
questions.why: The 180 km crater lies under the Yucatán Peninsula and the Gulf of Mexico, centred near the town of Chicxulub.

questions.q: The first skeleton of Archaeopteryx, the famous feathered “missing link” between dinosaurs and birds, was found in fine limestone quarries in 1861. Where?
questions.why: The Solnhofen limestone preserves fossils in exceptional detail; the London specimen arrived just two years after On the Origin of Species.

questions.q: Mary Anning found the first ichthyosaur skeleton to be correctly identified, and the first plesiosaurs, on the cliffs of her home town. Which?
questions.why: Anning collected fossils along the Jurassic Coast at Lyme Regis; her discoveries helped found the science of palaeontology.

questions.q: Charles Walcott discovered a fossil bed packed with bizarre 508-million-year-old sea creatures, high on a mountain ridge. Where?
questions.why: The Burgess Shale lies in the Canadian Rockies of Yoho National Park, British Columbia.

questions.q: A coelacanth — a fish thought extinct for 66 million years — was found in a trawler’s catch in 1938. Near which port?
questions.why: Museum curator Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer spotted the fish at East London; it was caught off the Chalumna River mouth.

questions.q: The first modern Olympic Games opened on 6 April 1896 in a restored ancient marble stadium. Where?
questions.why: The Panathenaic Stadium, rebuilt in marble, hosted the 1896 Games; it is still where the Olympic flame is handed over to each host city.

questions.q: The first FIFA World Cup final was played in 1930, with the hosts beating Argentina 4–2. In which stadium?
questions.why: Uruguay built the Estadio Centenario for the tournament, marking 100 years since its first constitution.

questions.q: Roger Bannister ran the first sub-four-minute mile on 6 May 1954. On which track?
questions.why: Bannister ran 3:59.4 at the Iffley Road track in Oxford, paced by Chris Brasher and Chris Chataway.

questions.q: The first official international football match, Scotland v England, ended 0–0 on 30 November 1872. In which city?
questions.why: The match was played at the West of Scotland Cricket Club ground, Hamilton Crescent, in Partick.

questions.q: The first Test cricket match, Australia v England, was played in March 1877 at which ground?
questions.why: Australia won by 45 runs at the MCG. The Centenary Test was played there in 1977 — with the same result.

questions.q: James Naismith invented basketball, nailing peach baskets to a gym balcony, at a YMCA training school in which city?
questions.why: Naismith devised the game in December 1891 at the International YMCA Training School (now Springfield College). The Basketball Hall of Fame is in the city.

questions.q: The first Winter Olympics were held in 1924 at a resort beneath Mont Blanc. Which?
questions.why: The “International Winter Sports Week” at Chamonix was retroactively named the first Winter Olympics.

questions.q: Usain Bolt set the 100 m world record of 9.58 seconds at the 2009 World Championships. In which stadium?
questions.why: Bolt ran 9.58 on 16 August 2009 in Berlin’s Olympiastadion, built for the 1936 Olympics.

questions.q: Diego Maradona scored both the “Hand of God” goal and the “Goal of the Century” against England at the 1986 World Cup. In which stadium?
questions.why: The quarter-final was played at the Estadio Azteca on 22 June 1986; Argentina won 2–1 and went on to lift the trophy.

questions.q: Pelé scored his 1,000th goal, a penalty against Vasco da Gama, on 19 November 1969. In which stadium?
questions.why: Pelé’s “Milésimo” came for Santos at the Maracanã; the ball was carried around the pitch in celebration.

questions.q: Muhammad Ali regained the world heavyweight title from George Foreman in the “Rumble in the Jungle” in 1974. In which city?
questions.place: Democratic Republic of the Congo (then Zaire)
questions.why: The fight took place before dawn on 30 October 1974 at the Stade du 20 Mai in Kinshasa; Ali won by knockout in the eighth round.

questions.q: A team of US college players beat the Soviet Union at ice hockey in the “Miracle on Ice” at the 1980 Winter Olympics. Where?
questions.why: The game was played on 22 February 1980 at Lake Placid in the Adirondack Mountains, which also hosted the 1932 Winter Games.

questions.q: New Zealand beat France in the final of the first Rugby World Cup in 1987. In which stadium?
questions.why: The All Blacks won 29–9 at Eden Park; New Zealand co-hosted the tournament with Australia.

questions.q: The first ever Formula One World Championship race was held on 13 May 1950 at a former RAF airfield. Which circuit?
questions.why: Giuseppe Farina won the 1950 British Grand Prix at Silverstone in an Alfa Romeo, and went on to become the first world champion.

questions.q: Eliud Kipchoge became the first person to run a marathon distance in under two hours, in a special event in 2019. In which city?
questions.why: Kipchoge ran 1:59:40 on laps of the Hauptallee in Vienna’s Prater park on 12 October 2019; it was not record-eligible because of the pacing.

questions.q: Ludwig Guttmann organised an archery contest for injured war veterans in 1948 — the forerunner of the Paralympic Games. At which hospital?
questions.why: The first Stoke Mandeville Games began on 29 July 1948, the same day as the London Olympics opened.

questions.q: The first Africa Cup of Nations, contested by just three teams and won by Egypt, was held in 1957. In which city?
questions.why: Egypt beat Ethiopia 4–0 in the final in Khartoum; South Africa had been expelled for refusing to field a multiracial team.

questions.q: The Beatles played nearly 300 times at a cellar club, where Brian Epstein first saw them in 1961. In which city?
questions.why: The Cavern Club on Mathew Street in Liverpool was where Epstein watched them on 9 November 1961 and soon became their manager.

questions.q: The 1969 Woodstock festival was not actually held in the town of Woodstock. On whose dairy farm did it take place?
questions.why: About 400,000 people gathered on Max Yasgur’s farm in Bethel, some 70 km from Woodstock itself.

questions.q: Alfred Nobel’s will asked for the Peace Prize to be awarded by a Norwegian committee. In which city was the first one presented, in 1901?
questions.why: The other prizes were presented in Stockholm; the Peace Prize was awarded in Kristiania (Oslo) — it still is, every 10 December.

questions.q: The first Eurovision Song Contest, with seven countries, was held in 1956 in which lakeside city?
questions.why: Lys Assia won for the host nation, Switzerland, at the Teatro Kursaal in Lugano.

questions.q: The world’s oldest film festival was first held in 1932 on the terrace of the Hotel Excelsior. In which city?
questions.why: The Venice Film Festival began as part of the Venice Biennale on the Lido, where it is still held each year.

questions.q: Raja Harishchandra, the first full-length Indian feature film, by Dadasaheb Phalke, premiered in 1913 in which city?
questions.why: Phalke’s silent film was shown at the Coronation Cinema in Bombay in May 1913 — the start of what became Bollywood.

questions.q: DJ Kool Herc’s “Back to School Jam” at 1520 Sedgwick Avenue in August 1973 is celebrated as the birth of hip hop. In which borough?
questions.why: Herc extended the instrumental breaks of funk records at a party in his building’s recreation room in the West Bronx.
